             MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                    SOUTHWEST POWER POOL, INC.

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (the “Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212

and 385.213, Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”) submits this Motion for Leave to Answer

and Answer1 in response to the comments and protests filed in regarding SPP’s response

to the request for additional information issued this proceeding.




1

       this proceeding to aid the Commission’s decision-making process. The
       Commission regularly permits answers for good cause shown, and the Commission
       has held that answers are permitted when they ensure a more accurate and complete
       record, clarify the issues, or provide useful and relevant information that will assist
       the Commission in its deliberative process. See, e.g., City Utils. of Springfield, Mo.
       v. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 168 FERC ¶ 61,085, at P 51 (2019) (“We accept the

 I.     BACKGROUND

       On April 17, 2026, pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)2 and

Part 35 of the Commission’s regulations,3 SPP submitted revisions to its Open Access

Transmission Tariff4 to (1) create a Peak Demand assessment (“PDA”) which compares

pre-season qualified capacity to actual, weather normalized Peak Demand; and (2) better

emulsifies demand response into SPP’s operations and resource adequacy framework.5 On

May 6, 2026, SPP amended its April Filing to modify Section 14 of Attachment AA to

include revisions within language specific to the SPP West Balancing Authority (“SPP

West BAA”).6

II.      ANSWER

      A. The protests and comments largely reiterate previous arguments, and fall
         short of identifying any new substantive concerns in SPP’s proposal.

         As an initial matter, it must be noted that, in large part, the protests and comments

filed in response to SPP’s Deficiency Response add little to the record. Rather than identify

new substantive concerns arising from SPP’s Deficiency Response, the protests and

comments largely reiterate objections which were raised (or could have been raised) in

response to SPP’s initial filing. Stated differently, the protests’ and comments’ continued

disagreement with SPP’s proposed revisions does not transform those previously-raised

 objections into new deficiencies, nor does it establish that SPP’s responses to the

Commission’s specified inquiries are inadequate. Having already presented their

objections to the underlying design, protestors cannot establish that SPP's Deficiency

Response is inadequate simply by restating those objections and asserting that they remain

unresolved. Rather, SPP requests that the Commission evaluate that record under the

applicable Section 205 standard and decline the protestors’ invitations to revisit previously-

articulated policy disagreements as though they constitute newly-identified deficiencies.26

     B. MMU

               1. The MMU fails to establish a lack of “adequate procedure.”27

       The MMU argues that SPP’s proposal to incorporate certain provisions of its

Business Practices into the Tariff through a Commission-directed compliance filing is

procedurally inadequate.28 The MMU's argument, however, conflates two distinct

questions: (1) whether particular provisions must be included in the Tariff under the rule

of reason; and (2) whether the Commission may direct SPP to incorporate provisions

through a compliance filing as a condition of accepting the proposed revisions.

Accordingly, and as described below, the MMU’s argument here fails.

       First, the Commission routinely accepts Section 205 filings subject to a compliance

filing, and that approach is consistent with its Section 205 authority where, as here, the

compliance filing implements language the filing utility itself has offered and does not

                                        Page 6 of 42
 reshape the proposal.29 Indeed, compliance filings are noticed by the Commission and open

to comment and protest.30 Therefore, contrary to the MMU’s argument, the MMU will

have the notice and opportunity it says it needs, and it will be able to review and protest

any actual Tariff language.31

       Second, the MMU's reliance on the rule of reason does not establish that a

Commission-directed compliance filing is an impermissible procedural mechanism. The

MMU cites City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368 (D.C. Cir. 1985), Southwest Power

Pool, Inc., 169 FERC ¶ 61,048 at P 62 (2019), and Energy Storage Association, 162 FERC

¶ 61,296 at P 104 (2018), for the proposition that requirements affecting resource eligibility

or market outcomes must be included in a tariff. But those decisions establish, at most, that

certain requirements are sufficiently significant to warrant inclusion in a Commission-

jurisdictional tariff. They do not establish that a Commission-directed compliance filing is

unavailable to remedy any omission of such requirements.

       Third, the MMU appears to argue 18 C.F.R. § 35.17(b) (entitled, “Amendments or

Modifications to Rate Schedule, Tariff or Service Agreement Sections Prior to

incorporating the identified provisions is through an amendment submitted before

Commission action on the underlying proposal.32 § 35.17(b) reads:

               (b) Amendments or modifications to rate schedule, tariff or
               service agreement sections prior to Commission action on
               the filing. A public utility may file to amend or modify, and
               may file a settlement that would amend or modify, a rate
               schedule, tariff or service agreement section contained in a
               rate schedule, tariff or service agreement filing that has not
               become effective and upon which no Commission or
               delegated order has yet been issued. Such filing will toll the
               notice period in section 205(d) of the Federal Power Act for
               the original filing, and establish a new date on which the
               entire filing will become effective, in the absence of
               Commission action, no earlier than 61 days from the date of
               the filing of the amendment or modification.

It is not clear how the fact that a regulation permits a public utility to amend a filing is

evidence of procedural impropriety here. Indeed, the MMU identifies no authority

establishing that the Commission is prohibited from accepting a proposed compliance

filing in this case. To the contrary, the Commission routinely accepts Section 205 filings

subject to a compliance filing where, as here, the required modifications are minor and do

not alter the fundamental design of the filing utility's proposal.33 Specifically, any

SPP has already identified, and would leave the substance and structure of SPP's proposal

unchanged. The MMU offers no persuasive reason why that mechanism would be

unavailable here, particularly where SPP has already identified the relevant Business

Practices and committed to incorporating them into the Tariff if directed by the

Commission.

        Fourth, the MMU overstates any perceived procedural prejudice by suggesting that

stakeholders cannot evaluate provisions that have not yet been incorporated into the Tariff.

The relevant Business Practices are not hypothetical provisions whose substance remains

unknown. They are existing, identifiable provisions. Indeed, the MMU's protests

throughout this docket demonstrate that the MMU understands the Business Practices’

contents and operational implications. The MMU identifies the precise demand response

cap, its allocation methodology, and the manner in which the applicable resource adequacy

requirement is determined.34 The MMU then advances detailed substantive objections to

each of those provisions.35 Thus, the MMU cannot credibly maintain that the absence of

those provisions from the Tariff has prevented it from understanding or challenging the

framework SPP proposes to implement.

        In short, the MMU's argument mistakes the requirement that certain provisions

appear in the Tariff for a requirement that the Commission cannot require a compliance

filing in this case. The former is a substantive obligation under the rule of reason; the latter

is a procedural limitation that the MMU has not established. Accordingly, SPP asks that

 the Commission reject the MMU's contention that a Commission-directed compliance

filing is inherently inadequate and instead evaluate SPP's proposal on its merits, subject to

any directive requiring incorporation of the identified Business Practices into the Tariff.

                 2. The MMU’s criticism of SPP’s proposed implementation date does
                    not undermine the reliability justifications for the proposed
                    revisions.

        The MMU contends that SPP’s proposed June 1, 2027, effective date is inconsistent

with SPP’s reliability justification because the proposed revisions would not apply during

the 2027 Summer Season. The MMU’s argument rests on the mistaken premise that a

reliability-driven proposal must be implemented at the earliest conceivable opportunity or

else the reliability concerns supporting it are not legitimate. Accordingly, and as described

in more detail below, the MMU’s argument fails.

        First, the implementation of new requirements require significant modifications to

existing processes and extensive work with SPP’s software vendor. These considerations

do not disappear merely because the revisions are intended to address reliability risks.

SPP’s recognition of those practical considerations does not diminish the underlying

reliability concerns. Rather, it reflects SPP’s effort to ensure that the proposed framework

can be implemented in an administratively workable manner. The MMU identifies no basis

for concluding that a reliability measure is unjustified merely because immediate

implementation is impracticable. Indeed, the MMU's position would produce an

unreasonable result: SPP would effectively be penalized for identifying a reliability

concern before it could reasonably implement the measures necessary to address that

concern. The Commission should not discourage proactive identification of reliability risks

by treating reasonable implementation timelines as evidence that those risks are

insignificant.
                                       Page 10 of 42
        Second, the MMU improperly treats SPP’s reliability analysis as a prediction of

specific reliability events rather than an assessment of the potential consequences of

increased reliance on Non-Registered Demand Response Programs. SPP's analysis

evaluates the reliability implications of different levels of load-modifying demand

response, including the potential consequences of allowing increased quantities of Non-

Registered Demand Response Programs to reduce Load Responsible Entity’s (“LRE”)

Peak Demand without corresponding operational visibility or demonstrated performance.

The analysis is intended to inform the development of a resource adequacy framework that

appropriately accounts for those risks. It does not purport to establish that a particular

number of emergency events will necessarily occur in a particular season absent immediate

implementation. The MMU's reliance on the greater number of projected emergency events

during the Summer Season therefore misses the point. That SPP's analysis identifies

comparatively greater reliability exposure during the Summer Season does not mean that

the proposed revisions cease to serve a legitimate reliability purpose if they cannot be

implemented before the 2027 Summer Season. Nor does the inability to mitigate every

identified risk immediately render subsequent mitigation ineffective or unnecessary. A

measure that reduces reliability exposure beginning in the 2027–2028 Winter Season and

in subsequent seasons remains valuable even if implementation constraints prevent it from

addressing the preceding Summer Season.

       Ultimately, the MMU's argument confuses the timing of a reliability improvement

with the existence of the reliability problem the improvement is designed to address. SPP

has identified a legitimate concern with allowing increasing quantities of Non-Registered

Demand Response Programs to reduce resource adequacy obligations without

corresponding operational visibility and performance accountability. The proposed
                                      Page 11 of 42
 revisions are intended to address that concern prospectively through a framework that

balances reliability, implementation feasibility, and LRE readiness. The MMU’s preference

for an earlier effective date, or its disagreement with particular modeling assumptions, does

not demonstrate that SPP's proposed framework is unjust and unreasonable.

               3. The transitional treatment of Non-Registered Demand Response
                  Programs is reasonably related to differences among LREs, and is
                  not unduly discriminatory.

       The MMU argues that SPP’s proposal impermissibly subjects LREs to different

resource adequacy requirements based on non-registered demand response forecasts

submitted in 2025.36 According to the MMU, because those forecasts were submitted

before LREs knew they would determine their eligibility for transitional treatment, they

cannot justify different treatment.37 This argument misunderstands both the purpose of the

temporary provisions and the significance of the historical forecasts.

       First, the fact that LREs may receive different treatment under a tariff does not,

standing alone, establish undue discrimination.38 Rather, differences in treatment are

permissible where they are reasonably related to relevant differences in circumstances.39

Here, the temporary provisions recognize that LREs entered the transition with differing

practical challenges in adjusting to the revised framework.

       Second, SPP’s use of 2025 resource adequacy workbook forecasts provides an

objective, preexisting benchmark for identifying those differences. Rather than allowing

LREs to establish new baselines after becoming aware of the proposed treatment, SPP

relies on information submitted before the transitional provisions were developed. This

approach limits the opportunity for LREs to alter their reported reliance on non-registered

       Third, and relatedly, the MMU’s observation that LREs did not know their 2025

forecasts would later be used for this purpose cuts against its own argument. Because the

forecasts preceded the proposed policy, they were not developed in anticipation of the

transitional treatment. Their use provides a reasonable means of establishing a historical

baseline without inviting the strategic adjustments that might accompany a newly

established reporting opportunity. Nor does the MMU establish that the proposal creates

two fundamentally different resource adequacy constructs. All LREs remain subject to the

overarching requirements of Attachment AA of the Tariff. The temporary provisions

address the treatment of specified demand-related inputs during the transition, rather than

creating entirely separate resource adequacy programs. The fact that an input may be

determined differently for particular LREs does not mean that the underlying resource

adequacy framework is discriminatory.

       Finally, the temporary nature of the provisions is significant. The provisions

establish a limited transition designed to recognize existing practices while moving LREs

toward a more consistent framework. The MMU's preferred approach would effectively

disregard those differences and require immediate uniform treatment notwithstanding the
                                      Page 13 of 42
 practical consequences of transitioning from existing arrangements. The FPA does not

require such an inflexible result.40 Rather, the relevant question is whether SPP's temporary

distinctions are reasonably related to legitimate resource adequacy and implementation

considerations.

               4. The MMU has not demonstrated that SPP’s weather normalization
                  framework creates unreasonable opportunities for gaming.

       The MMU contends that SPP’s proposed weather normalization framework is

inadequate because SPP's ability to reproduce an LRE’s calculation does not establish that

the underlying methodology is reasonable.41 The MMU further argues that state regulatory

oversight does not provide a sufficient safeguard because not all LREs are subject to such

oversight and the methodologies used in state proceedings may differ from those submitted

to SPP.42 For the reasons set forth below, these arguments are unpersuasive.

       First, the MMU's argument improperly equates methodological discretion with an

absence of meaningful accountability. The fact that LREs may employ different weather

normalization methodologies does not establish that those methodologies are inherently

unreliable or that the resulting resource adequacy determinations will be unreasonable.

Indeed, the MMU’s position is difficult to reconcile with its own approach to evaluating

mitigated offers in SPP's Integrated Marketplace. In that context, Market Participants may

employ different methodologies and rely on resource-specific assumptions to calculate the

costs underlying their mitigated offers. The MMU does not insist that every Market

 Participant employs an identical methodology or that the mere existence of methodological

discretion renders those calculations unreliable. Rather, the applicable framework

establishes requirements governing the development and documentation of those

calculations and provides mechanisms for reviewing whether the resulting offers comply

with those requirements.

       The same principle applies here. SPP's ability to reproduce an LRE's weather

normalization calculation is not intended, standing alone, to establish the substantive

reasonableness of every methodological choice. Rather, reproducibility provides an

important measure of transparency and accountability by allowing SPP to verify the inputs,

assumptions, and calculations underlying an LRE's submission. Thus, the MMU has not

demonstrated that the existence of methodological discretion, by itself, renders SPP's

proposed framework unjust and unreasonable.

       Second, the MMU's criticism of SPP's reference to state regulatory oversight does

not establish that the proposed framework is deficient. SPP has not represented that every

LRE is subject to identical state regulatory requirements. Rather, the existence of external

review processes for certain LREs provides additional context for evaluating their

established forecasting practices. The fact that those processes are not universal does not

establish that LREs operating outside such processes necessarily employ unreasonable

methodologies. Nor does the possibility that an LRE might use different methodologies for

different regulatory purposes demonstrate impropriety. Forecasting methodologies may

reasonably differ depending on the purpose of the forecast, the relevant measurement

period, and the regulatory requirements involved. The MMU identifies no specific instance

in which an LRE has employed inconsistent methodologies to manipulate its resource

adequacy obligation.
                                      Page 15 of 42
        Third, the MMU's allegations of gaming are speculative, and the MMU has not

demonstrated that LREs are likely to manipulate their calculations to avoid deficiency

payments. The mere possibility that an LRE could exercise methodological discretion

improperly does not establish that the framework itself is unjust and unreasonable.

Additionally, the LREs are required to provide their weather normalization methodologies

prior to each season when their actual peak demand is assessed for the deficiency payment.

This decreases gaming potential of actual load values after the season.

               5. The MMU mischaracterizes Firm Service Level as an arbitrary
                  value determined by LREs.

       The MMU contends that SPP’s explanation of Firm Service Level is insufficient

because the expected load component may vary from season to season and is not

independently established through capability testing.43 According to the MMU, this permits

LREs to effectively determine their own accredited demand response capability.44 The

MMU's argument, however, overlooks the relationship between Firm Service Level, Net

Generating Capability, and the broader resource adequacy calculation.

       First, as SPP explained in its Deficiency Response, Firm Service Level represents

a resource’s expected load after deployment to its Net Generating Capability. The MMU

acknowledges that Net Generating Capability is established through the applicable testing

requirements in the SPP Planning Criteria. Thus, the proposed framework does not permit

an LRE to establish accredited capability merely by selecting an unsupported Firm Service

Level value.




43
       MMU Protest at 14.
44
       Id.

                                      Page 16 of 42
         Second, the fact that expected load may change from season to season does not

render the resulting Firm Service Level arbitrary. Demand response may serve customers

or facilities whose expected consumption varies based on seasonal conditions, operating

schedules, or other relevant factors. A calculation that accounts for those variations may

more accurately represent the Resource's operating characteristics than one that assumes a

fixed load level regardless of changing circumstances. Indeed, the MMU’s suggestion that

seasonal variability itself undermines the calculation would effectively require SPP to

disregard changes in expected load that may be relevant to evaluating the Resource. Such

an approach would not necessarily improve the accuracy of resource accreditation.

        Finally, the MMU prematurely dismisses the significance of proposed Attachment

AA, Section 12.2 of the Tariff, which requires the actual metered load for the applicable

interval to be compared to the projected Firm Service Level to determine how much to add

back when determining an LRE’s Post-Season Net Peak Demand. This provision is an

important component of the overall framework. By considering the Firm Service Level in

the demand calculation, the proposal coordinates the treatment of demand response

capability with the corresponding demand obligations.

     C. Transmission Owners (“TO Group”)

               1. The TO Group’s Protest largely reiterates previously-raised
                  objections and fails to demonstrate that SPP’s deficiency response is
                  inadequate.

        The TO Group’s latest Protest largely repeats arguments it previously presented in

its May 27, 2026, Protest and June 30, 2026, Answer.45 Thus, although framed as a

               2. Voltus’ preferred alternative accreditation methodology is beyond
                  the scope of the Commission’s review under Section 205.

       Voltus’ proposed alternative accreditation methodology provides no basis for

rejecting or modifying SPP’s filing. Under Section 205 of the FPA, the Commission’s

inquiry is whether the rate, term, or condition proposed by the filing utility is just and

reasonable—not whether a protestant has identified an alternative approach that it believes

would be preferable. The Commission need not determine that SPP’s proposal represents

the optimal accreditation methodology, nor must it evaluate the relative merits of every

alternative advanced by protestors.76 Rather, where the filing utility demonstrates that its

proposed revisions are just and reasonable, the Commission may accept those revisions

notwithstanding the existence of other potentially just and reasonable approaches.77

        Here, Voltus advocates for a materially different methodology under which Net

Generating Capability would be calculated as the difference between an LRE-assigned

seasonal baseline and a resource-elected Firm Service Level, rather than determined

through SPP’s Capability Test framework. Voltus supports its preferred approach by

reference to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s demand response accreditation practices and

asserts that its methodology would provide greater predictability and more accurately

reflect a resource’s contribution to resource adequacy. But even assuming, arguendo, that

market design for a just and reasonable proposal submitted by the filing utility. The relevant

inquiry is whether SPP has adequately supported its proposed accreditation framework—

not whether another framework might also be reasonable or offer different advantages.
